title: How do the commentators differ on this verse?

messages.text: How do the commentators differ on this verse?

Commentators agree the verse is a promise to believers, not a claim that everything is good in itself — but they part on what "his purpose" means, and on a reading of the Greek.

**What "called according to his purpose" means**
- Gill reads it as God's eternal purpose of election: those called are the ones chosen before the world began, so the promise is sure for them and them only.
- Barnes also sees God's plan behind the call, but stresses that it is shown in their love for God, which the verse names first.
- Clarke disagrees: he takes the purpose as God's plan to call Gentiles as well as Jews by the gospel, and says nothing here settles who will finally be saved.
- Wesley is close to Clarke: the called are those who answer the call and love God, and the promise is theirs while they continue to.

**Who does the working**
- Vincent and A.T. Robertson note that some early manuscripts add "God" as the subject: "God works all things together for good." Robertson thinks the sense is the same either way, since it is God at work.
- JFB keeps the usual reading, with "all things" as the subject, but says it is God who makes them work together.

**Not really in dispute**
"All things" includes suffering: Henry, Barnes and JFB all read it with the groaning and weakness of verses 18 to 26, and none takes it to mean the believer will be spared trouble.
